title: Non-Empty String
story: A payment processor once sent invoices with empty customer names because the UI allowed blank submissions. A single `NonEmptyStr` type would have prevented every blank invoice from entering the system.
why: Domain types with invariants make invalid states impossible to represent, eliminating entire categories of bugs.
analogy: A `NonEmptyStr` is like a sealed envelope — you know it contains something before you open it, so you never handle empty mail.
try_it: Add a `NonEmptyStr.concat` method that takes `&self` and another `&NonEmptyStr`, returns a new `NonEmptyStr`. Since both inputs are guaranteed non-empty, the result is guaranteed non-empty — no check needed!
tips: Use `Option` in constructors when input might be invalid — let the caller handle the failure case
Chain NonEmptyStr methods fearlessly — each method's output respects the invariant
The invariant eliminates defensive `if value == ""` checks everywhere downstream
common_mistakes: Returning `NonEmptyStr` from a constructor without actually building a valid one — the invariant check will catch it but the panic is confusing
Treating invariant types as 'optional checks' — if you bypass the constructor with a raw struct literal, the invariant is your last line of defense
